{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in group theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Tits alternative''', named after [[Jacques Tits]], is an important theorem about the structure of [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] [[linear group]]s.

==Statement==

The theorem, proven by Tits,<ref name=T72>{{cite journal|last = Tits|first = J.|title = Free subgroups in linear groups|journal = [[Journal of Algebra]]|volume = 20|year = 1972 | pages = 250–270|doi = 10.1016/0021-8693(72)90058-0 | issue = 2 | doi-access = free}}</ref> is stated as follows.

{{math theorem | Let <math>G</math> be a [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] [[linear group]] over a field. Then two following possibilities occur:
*either <math>G</math> is [[virtually]] [[solvable group|solvable]] (i.e., has a solvable [[subgroup]] of [[finite index]])
*or it contains a nonabelian [[free group]] (i.e., it has a [[subgroup]] [[Group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the free group on two generators).}}

==Consequences==

A linear group is not [[Amenable group|amenable]] if and only if it contains a non-abelian free group (thus the [[von Neumann conjecture]], while not true in general, holds for linear groups).

The Tits alternative is an important ingredient<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tits |first=Jacques |date=1981 |title=Groupes à croissance polynomiale |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/?id=SB_1980-1981__23__176_0 |journal=Séminaire Bourbaki |language=French |volume=1980/1981}}</ref> in the proof of [[Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth]]. In fact the alternative essentially establishes the result for linear groups (it reduces it to the case of solvable groups, which can be dealt with by elementary means).

==Generalizations==

In [[geometric group theory]], a group ''G'' is said to '''satisfy the Tits alternative''' if for every [[subgroup]] ''H'' of ''G'' either ''H'' is virtually solvable or ''H'' contains a [[abelian group|nonabelian]] free [[subgroup]] (in some versions of the definition this condition is only required to be satisfied for all [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] subgroups of ''G'').

Examples of groups satisfying the Tits alternative which are either not linear, or at least not known to be linear, are:

*[[Hyperbolic group]]s
*[[Mapping class group]]s;<ref>{{cite journal | last=Ivanov | first=Nikolai | title=Algebraic properties of the Teichmüller modular group | journal=Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR | volume=275 | year=1984 | pages=786–789}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=McCarthy | first=John | title=A "Tits-alternative" for subgroups of surface mapping class groups | journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. | volume=291 | year=1985 | issue=2 | pages=583–612 | doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1985-0800253-8| doi-access=free }}</ref>
*[[Out(Fn)]];<ref>{{cite journal|last = [[Mladen Bestvina|Bestvina]]|first = Mladen |author2=Feighn, Mark |author3=Handel, Michael|title = The Tits alternative for Out(''F<sub>n</sub>'') I: Dynamics of exponentially-growing automorphisms|journal = [[Annals of Mathematics]]|volume = 151|year = 2000|pages = 517–623|arxiv = math/9712217|doi = 10.2307/121043|jstor =121043|issue = 2}}</ref>
*Certain groups of [[rational mapping|birational transformations]] of [[algebraic surface]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Cantat | first=Serge | title=Sur les groupes de transformations birationnelles des surfaces | journal=Ann. Math. | volume=174 | date=2011 | pages=299–340 | language=French | doi=10.4007/annals.2011.174.1.8| doi-access=free }}</ref>

Examples of groups not satisfying the Tits alternative are:

*the [[Grigorchuk group]];
*[[Thompson groups|Thompson's group ''F'']].

==Proof==

The proof of the original Tits alternative<ref name=T72/> is by looking at the [[Zariski topology|Zariski closure]] of <math>G</math> in <math>\mathrm{GL}_n(k)</math>. If it is solvable then the group is solvable. Otherwise one looks at the image of <math>G</math> in the Levi component. If it is noncompact then a [[Ping-pong lemma|ping-pong]] argument finishes the proof. If it is compact then either all eigenvalues of elements in the image of <math>G</math> are roots of unity and then the image is finite, or one can find an embedding of <math>k</math> in which one can apply the ping-pong strategy.

Note that the proof of all generalisations above also rests on a ping-pong argument.
